metadata.title: Two Resolutions, One Click — The macOS Coordinate Roundtrip.
metadata.purpose: Take apart the macOS coordinate roundtrip: explain the tile-budget constraint that forces the reference client to resize a Retina screenshot before sending, evaluate the ratio-based inverse that recovers the real click, and name the boundary case where the multiplier collapses to one. Land the carry-out that a Claude coordinate on macOS isn't wrong — it's measured on a resized copy of your Retina screen, and multiplying back by native over sent puts the click on the button.
metadata.one_flag: none - fully derived from the documented target_image_size constraints, see SOURCES.md

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. Claude never sees your 2560 by 1600 Retina screen — the reference client resizes it to 1344 by 840 first. The 630, 420 lives inside that smaller picture. The real screen coordinate isn't in the answer; it's in the ratio you have to multiply back.

beats.narration_text: Here's the constraint that forces a transform. A Retina screenshot is 2560 by 1600 on many MacBook Pros. The API's image budget won't take that: the long edge has to stay under 1568 pixels, and the picture can't cross more than 1568 of the model's 28 by 28 tiles. The reference client's answer is to resize before sending — down to 1344 by 840. They optimized for a predictable tile budget at the expense of the pixel-perfect frame the OS actually rendered. Same button now lives in two coordinate spaces, and only one of them touches your screen.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — two rectangles, 2560x1600 native and 1344x840 sent, same button dot, bridged by a question mark

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — two spaces, one button
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. Left rectangle labelled '2560 × 1600 — native Retina' with a terracotta button dot. Right rectangle labelled '1344 × 840 — sent to API', smaller, same aspect ratio. A question-mark arrow bridges them. THIS EXACT PAIR OF RECTANGLES RETURNS AT B04.

beats.narration_text: The natural guess is to click Claude's number directly — the model saw the button, so its coordinate must be the button. It isn't. Click 630, 420 on the real 2560 by 1600 screen and you land somewhere else entirely. That number was never a screen coordinate; it was a pixel address inside the resized picture Claude got shown. Same numeric pair, wrong canvas — an unavoidable side-effect of shipping the model a downsized copy without telling it the copy was downsized.

shot.new_visual_element: Same anchor pair; raw (630,420) carried straight across onto the 2560x1600 rectangle — misses the button, struck

production_viz.label: Same raw pixel, wrong canvas
production_viz.mechanic: The B01 rectangle pair returns. The (630, 420) dot is carried across unscaled onto the 2560×1600 rectangle; it lands short of a target ring near center, marked with a cross. Caption: 'nowhere close to the button'.

beats.narration_text: The fix ports the API's own resize algorithm back into the client. A binary search for the largest width and height that keep the aspect ratio, hold the long edge under 1568 pixels, and stay under 1568 tiles. For a 2560 by 1600 screen it converges on 1344 by 840. Record those sent dimensions — they're the denominator of the inverse: real equals model, times native, divided by sent. They chose to bake the same clamping rule on both sides of the wire instead of returning the sent size in a response header — a simpler protocol, at the cost of every caller having to re-implement the ratio themselves.

shot.new_visual_element: Formula card: real = model x (native / sent), worked to 2560x1600 -> 1344x840; source credit

production_viz.label: The inverse ratio
production_viz.mechanic: Two formula lines build in ink mono on cream: 'real_x = model_x × (native_w / sent_w)' then 'real_y = model_y × (native_h / sent_h)'. Beneath, a smaller terracotta line: '2560×1600 → sent 1344×840'. Caption bottom-right: 'Source: Claude Quickstarts (Anthropic)'.

beats.narration_text: Run it against Claude's own click. 630 times 2560 over 1344 lands at 1200. 420 times 1600 over 840 lands at 800. The pointer sits on the button. Now the boundary case: if a screenshot already fits the budget, target underscore image underscore size leaves it alone — sent equals native, and the ratio collapses to one. Multiplying by one is a no-op, so the same code path handles the shrunk and the un-shrunk display without a special case. This works if you value one transform that always runs; it fails if you needed the API to just hand back the sent size in the first place.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — same rectangle pair, dot now scaled and lands on target; a second small card beside it: already fits, no resize needed

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — scaled, and it lands
production_viz.mechanic: THE B01/B02 RECTANGLE PAIR RETURNS, identical. This time (630, 420) is carried across with the ratio applied, landing exactly on the target ring at '(1200, 800)' inside the 2560×1600 rectangle, marked with a check. Off to the side, a second small card, not struck, captioned 'already fits the budget → sent = native, nothing to invert' — the boundary case, not an error.

beats.narration_text: A Claude coordinate on macOS isn't wrong — it's measured on a resized copy of your Retina screen. Multiply back by native over sent, and the click lands exactly where you meant.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I'm using Anthropic's computer-use tool on a MacBook Pro with a 2560 by 1600 Retina screen, and Claude's click coordinates never land where I expect. Explain exactly how the reference client resizes screenshots before sending them to the API — the target underscore image underscore size algorithm, the long-edge limit under 1568 pixels, the 1568-tile budget, and why my display resolves to 1344 by 840. Then write me a Python function that takes model_x, model_y, native width, native height, sent width, sent height, and returns the real screen coordinate, handling the boundary case where sent equals native. Finally, show the math end to end on my exact screen: Claude reports 630, 420 — where does the real click land? Go deeper: ask the same model what happens when a second display gets plugged in with a different aspect ratio, whether the resize algorithm has to be recomputed per screenshot or can be cached per display, and where in the capture pipeline the sent dimensions should be recorded so a later click doesn't inverse-transform against the wrong denominator.
